Trump’s Oil Protectorate

The Trump administration is negotiating for a long-term U.S. stake in 17 Venezuelan oil fields containing about 90 billion barrels of crude. That is roughly one-third of Venezuela’s proven reserves and could more than double the oil reserves available to the United States.

The deal under discussion is not a clean market investment. Washington would secure ownership or long leases, possibly lasting up to 100 years, then invite U.S. companies to develop the fields. Venezuela would keep a share of revenue. The United States would get the risk, the contracts and the part where the flag goes on the map.

There is a small engineering issue. Several of the 17 fields lack pipelines, treatment plants or transport access. Others have been stripped by neglect and theft. Private firms would need billions of dollars, security forces and a lawyer with a high pain tolerance. Venezuela’s oil output has risen only about 200,000 barrels in the past year despite promises that Maduro’s removal would unleash a drilling boom.

Marco Rubio and Energy Secretary Chris Wright reportedly hope to announce a deal in Venezuela early next month. But the interim government of Delcy Rodríguez may lack the constitutional authority to hand over strategic assets. Banks see a contract. Venezuelans may see a century-long invoice from a country that arrived promising democracy.

Trump built his foreign policy around “America First.” Now America may become a minority shareholder in the world’s messiest oil company.

The White House says it wants energy security. Caracas gets a new supervisor. U.S. taxpayers get to find out whether 90 billion barrels can cover the cost of owning the headache.

Trump’s Iran Victory Tour: One Problem — The Victory


Six months ago, Trump promised Iran a quick lesson in the consequences of challenging the United States. The bombs arrived. The missiles flew. Iranian military and nuclear infrastructure was hammered. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed. The message from Washington was unmistakable: this would be decisive.

And then, rather inconveniently, Iran failed to read the script.

Six months later, Tehran is battered but still standing. Its economy is under extraordinary pressure, inflation is soaring, food prices have exploded, military infrastructure has been badly damaged — and yet Iran has not surrendered, signed the deal Trump wanted, or simply gone home.

Instead, the Strait of Hormuz has become Tehran’s favorite bargaining chip, turning a narrow stretch of water into one of the most consequential pieces of real estate in global politics. Nothing says “quick and easy victory” quite like a war in which everyone suddenly starts worrying about the price of oil.

Washington’s response? More sanctions.

When military pressure failed to produce the desired political outcome, the administration turned increasingly to economic coercion — the familiar instrument of a government discovering that destroying an adversary is considerably easier than persuading it to surrender.

The original promise was simple: overwhelming American power would force Iran to capitulate. The reality has proved considerably messier. 

Iran has taken extraordinary punishment, but it has also demonstrated the classic survival skill of an embattled regime: refusing to cooperate with the enemy’s definition of victory.

Diplomacy has not exactly been a triumph either. The June ceasefire and subsequent negotiating effort failed to produce a lasting settlement.

Mediation efforts involving Oman, Pakistan and Qatar have gone nowhere. Washington and Tehran continue to disagree over sanctions, the blockade, the Strait of Hormuz and the fundamental terms of any agreement.

Trump now faces the strategic question that every president eventually encounters after starting a war: How do you get out?

It is a particularly awkward question for a president who built much of his political identity around ending America’s endless wars.

The irony is difficult to miss. Trump promised to use American strength to prevent another Middle Eastern quagmire. Six months later, the United States is trying to turn military devastation into political leverage, economic pressure into surrender, and a war that was supposed to be short into something resembling an exit strategy.

Iran has certainly paid an enormous price. There is no serious argument otherwise.

But Iran has not collapsed.

And Washington has not yet produced the clean political victory that all those missiles were supposed to buy.

So perhaps the most revealing measure is not how many Iranian targets were destroyed, but how many months later we are still asking the same question: When exactly does the victory begin?

Because at the moment, Trump has won the bombing campaign. Iran has won the irritating privilege of still being there.

Time and again, the Middle East has once again declined to follow the PowerPoint presentation.
